marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q015.takeaway: Extensor carpi radialis longus arises from the lateral supracondylar ridge and inserts at the base of the second metacarpal.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q015.displayText:
The arrow indicates extensor carpi radialis longus. It originates from the distal third of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus and inserts at the base of the second metacarpal on the radial side.

It is innervated by the radial nerve (C6-C7), receives vascular supply from the radial recurrent artery, and extends and abducts the wrist.
emphasis: The arrow indicates extensor carpi radialis longus
It originates from the distal third of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus and inserts at the base of the second metacarpal on the radial side
It is innervated by the radial nerve (C6-C7), receives vascular supply from the radial recurrent artery, and extends and abducts the wrist

rationales.b: Brachioradialis lies laterally but inserts on distal radius near the styloid, not second metacarpal.
rationales.c: Supinator wraps the proximal radius and rotates the forearm; it is not the wrist extensor indicated.
rationales.d: Flexor carpi radialis is a wrist flexor inserting on metacarpal bases, and “brevis” is not the depicted muscle.

marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q016.takeaway: Palmar interossei are unipennate; dorsal interossei and medial lumbricals are bipennate in the source description.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q016.displayText:
Palmar interossei are unipennate muscles. Dorsal interossei and the medial two lumbricals are bipennate; the lateral two lumbricals and palmar interossei are unipennate.

A bipennate muscle has fibres converging on both sides of a central tendon.

rationales.c: The third lumbrical is one of the medial bipennate lumbricals.

marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q017.takeaway: Palmar interossei attach to the second, fourth and fifth metacarpals; the third metacarpal lacks a palmar-interosseous attachment.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q017.displayText:
The image demonstrates the card test for palmar interossei. The third metacarpal of the middle finger has no palmar-interosseous attachment.

Palmar interossei lie on the palmar surfaces of the metacarpals. They arise from the second metacarpal (ulnar side), fourth metacarpal (radial side), and fifth metacarpal (radial side). The source notes that a fourth palmar interosseous muscle is present in some people.
emphasis: The image demonstrates the card test for palmar interossei
The third metacarpal of the middle finger has no palmar-interosseous attachment
Palmar interossei lie on the palmar surfaces of the metacarpals

rationales.a: The fourth metacarpal has an attachment from a palmar interosseous.
rationales.b: The second metacarpal has an ulnar-side palmar-interosseous attachment.
rationales.d: The fifth metacarpal has a radial-side palmar-interosseous attachment.

marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q018.takeaway: Lumbricals flex the MCP joint and extend the IP joints by inserting into the dorsal digital expansion.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q018.displayText:
The muscle marked A is a lumbrical. Lumbricals flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints through the dorsal digital expansion.

They originate from flexor digitorum profundus. The lateral two are unipennate and supplied by the median nerve; the medial two are bipennate and supplied by the ulnar nerve.
emphasis: The muscle marked A is a lumbrical
Lumbricals flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints through the dorsal digital expansion
They originate from flexor digitorum profundus

rationales.b: Extension is not the lumbricals’ action at the MCP joint.
rationales.c: Adduction is a palmar-interosseous action, not the lumbrical MCP action.
rationales.d: Abduction is chiefly associated with dorsal interossei.

marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q019.takeaway: The middle finger has no palmar-interosseous attachment, so the second palmar interosseous does not contribute to its extensor expansion.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q019.displayText:
The marked structure is the dorsal digital expansion of the middle finger. A palmar interosseous muscle does not attach to the middle finger and therefore does not contribute to its dorsal digital expansion.

Palmar interossei are unipennate and adduct the digits. The middle finger has no palmar interosseous muscle. Dorsal interossei are bipennate and abduct the digits; they attach to the middle three fingers.

rationales.a: The second dorsal interosseous attaches to the middle-finger side and contributes to its expansion.
rationales.b: Lumbricals insert into the digital expansion.
rationales.c: Extensor digitorum tendon expands over the digit to form the extensor mechanism.

marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q020.takeaway: Intrinsic hand muscles (lumbricals and interossei) flex MCP joints and extend IP joints; their loss produces MCP extension with IP flexion.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q020.displayText:
The lumbricals and interossei are affected. Through their attachments to the dorsal digital expansions they flex the MCP joints and extend the IP joints.

With ulnar nerve injury these intrinsic muscles may atrophy, producing extension at the MCP joints and flexion at the IP joints. The source notes that the ulnar nerve supplies all intrinsic hand muscles except the first and second lumbricals, abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, and part of flexor pollicis brevis.
emphasis: The lumbricals and interossei are affected
Through their attachments to the dorsal digital expansions they flex the MCP joints and extend the IP joints
With ulnar nerve injury these intrinsic muscles may atrophy, producing extension at the MCP joints and flexion at the IP joints

rationales.a: Extensor digitorum extends MCP joints and contributes to IP extension; it is not the intrinsic muscle group lost in claw posture.
rationales.c: Abductor pollicis acts on the thumb, not the finger MCP/IP posture described.
rationales.d: Abductor pollicis brevis is a thenar thumb muscle, unrelated to the four-finger imbalance.

marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q021.takeaway: Opponens pollicis inserts along the lateral border and adjacent palmar surface of the first metacarpal to produce opposition.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q021.displayText:
The marked area is the palmar aspect of the first metacarpal. Opponens pollicis inserts here.

Opponens pollicis originates from the tubercle of trapezium and flexor retinaculum, inserts along the lateral border and adjoining lateral half of the palmar aspect of the first metacarpal, and flexes the first metacarpal bone of the thumb as part of opposition.
emphasis: The marked area is the palmar aspect of the first metacarpal
Opponens pollicis inserts here

Opponens pollicis originates from the tubercle of trapezium and flexor retinaculum, inserts along the lateral border and adjoining lateral half of the palmar aspect of the first metacarpal, and flexes the first metacarpal bone of the thumb as part of opposition

rationales.a: Abductor pollicis longus inserts at the base of the first metacarpal, not along its palmar border.
rationales.b: Palmar interossei attach to the second, fourth and fifth metacarpals rather than the first.
rationales.d: Flexor pollicis brevis inserts on the proximal phalanx of the thumb.

marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q022.takeaway: Power grip relies chiefly on extrinsic long flexors whose muscle bellies lie in the forearm.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q022.displayText:
Power grip is produced by the extrinsic muscles of the hand, especially the long flexors. Extrinsic muscles originate in the forearm and insert into the hand.

Precision grip is primarily a function of intrinsic hand muscles such as adductor pollicis, palmaris brevis, interossei, lumbricals, thenar and hypothenar muscles.
emphasis: Power grip is produced by the extrinsic muscles of the hand, especially the long flexors
Extrinsic muscles originate in the forearm and insert into the hand
Precision grip is primarily a function of intrinsic hand muscles such as adductor pollicis, palmaris brevis, interossei, lumbricals, thenar and hypothenar muscles

rationales.b: Short flexors are intrinsic muscles and contribute more to precise positioning than the main power-grip force.
rationales.c: Palmaris brevis wrinkles/tenses hypothenar skin and does not generate power grip.
rationales.d: Lumbricals coordinate MCP flexion/IP extension, rather than providing the principal forceful grasp.

marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q023.takeaway: The second lumbrical is supplied by the median nerve; the medial two lumbricals receive ulnar innervation.
marrow__ANAT_CH39_Q023.displayText:
The marked structure is the second lumbrical, which is supplied by the median nerve. The lateral two lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve and the medial two by the ulnar nerve.

Lumbricals flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend both interphalangeal joints.
emphasis: The marked structure is the second lumbrical, which is supplied by the median nerve
The lateral two lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve and the medial two by the ulnar nerve
Lumbricals flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend both interphalangeal joints

rationales.a: Posterior interosseous nerve supplies posterior forearm extensors, not lumbricals.
rationales.c: Anterior interosseous nerve supplies deep anterior forearm muscles, not the second lumbrical.
rationales.d: Ulnar nerve supplies the medial two lumbricals, not the second lateral lumbrical.
